audits.claim: The Old Tibetan Annals entries for 654-655 describe administrative preparation and the writing of laws.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved_full_text (52-page author-hosted PDF; pdftotext extraction; pdf sha256 a604dc8e2d19b5e3ecdfc16dbab57844ce85db83152377057127fe732de749c9)
audits.source_locator: van Schaik 2011, printed p. 53 (quotes of P.t.1288, ll.26-29; extraction lines 388-393)
audits.source_excerpt: [655] The year of the hare arrived. During this year the Tsenpo resided at Merkhe and Prime Minister Tongtsen wrote the texts of the laws at Gorti.
audits.basis: Same page gives the 654 entry: division into soldiers/civilians and preparation of the administrative manuals. van Schaik notes these dates fall after Songtsen Gampo's death, which matches the entry's framing.
audits.access_limit: Author-hosted copy of the published chapter; page images not inspected, text read from pdftotext extraction.

audits.claim: The 654-655 Annals entries are records of events in those years, not surviving physical manuscripts written in those years.
audits.source_locator: van Schaik 2011, printed p. 54 (extraction lines 455-460); related statements at p. 56 (extraction line 538 region)
audits.source_excerpt: Yet these inscriptions and documents date from the second half of the eighth century at the earliest, more than a century after the inception of writing in Tibet.
audits.basis: Same passage: 'we should not assume the earliest extant manuscripts reflect the use of writing over a century earlier'; earliest ink documents date to the latter part of the eighth century at the earliest (p. 56).
audits.access_limit: Author-hosted copy; the dating of individual Dunhuang manuscripts was not independently checked beyond this study.

audits.claim: van Schaik treats the Pillar Testament and Testament of Ba as important Thonmi-story witnesses, and the claim that the fourteenth-century historian Buton supplies its earliest version should not be repeated.
audits.source_excerpt: Butön’s fourteenth-century history of Buddhism has been presented as the earliest version of the Tönmi story, but this is not the case.
audits.basis: Continues: 'The earliest sources of the Tönmi story are the treasure text known as The Pillar Testament and the clan history called Testament of Ba.' Entry citation 49-54 matches the passage.
audits.access_limit: Author-hosted published chapter; page images not inspected, text read from pdftotext extraction.

audits.claim: The same study discusses the Zhol pillar as approximately 767.
audits.source_locator: van Schaik 2011, printed p. 51 (extraction line 318); variant phrasing 'dates from the 760s' at printed p. 56 (extraction line 538)
audits.source_excerpt: the monumental inscribed pillar that stands in front of the Potala in Lhasa, known as the Zhol pillar and dated to circa 767
audits.basis: The entry's 'approximately 767' matches 'circa 767'; the same study elsewhere says the pillar 'dates from the 760s', which is consistent with an approximate date.
audits.access_limit: Epigraphic dating accepted from this study; no independent epigraphic source was retrieved.

audits.claim: Received grammatical treatises attributed to Thonmi show post-imperial writing or rewriting.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/tibet.md:40 (section 2 table row, 'Did the founder write the grammars?')
audits.source_excerpt: the versions that have come down to us bear the signs of having been written, or at least rewritten, after the Tibetan imperial period
audits.basis: Preceding sentence notes modern scholars, including Tibetans, question even Tonmi's historical existence; supports the table's calibration column.
audits.access_limit: Same author-hosted chapter; philological arguments not independently re-run.

audits.claim: van Schaik argues for North Indian/Nepalese models for the Tibetan script, not an uncontested exact prototype.
audits.source_locator: van Schaik 2011, printed p. 46 (extraction lines 52-60); Part II weighing of the Northwest hypothesis at pp. 63-65 (extraction lines 848-890)
audits.source_excerpt: the North Indian and Nepalese inscriptions provide by far the best models for the Tibetan script
audits.basis: Introduction states the exact source of the alphabet is uncertain; Part II rejects a Northwest/Kashmir derivation on political and palaeographical grounds. Entry's 'not an uncontested exact prototype' is consistent.
audits.access_limit: Author-hosted chapter; the underlying paleographic tables were not re-verified.

audits.claim: A letter reportedly sent abroad need not have been written in Tibetan; Chinese-language diplomatic literacy is not proof of a Tibetan-script autograph.
audits.source_excerpt: such a letter would almost certainly have been written in Chinese, not Tibetan
audits.basis: Refers to the Tang Annals report of Songtsen Gampo's 634 letter requesting a Chinese princess; the paper uses it only as evidence that writing technology was present, exactly the entry's caution.
audits.access_limit: Author-hosted chapter; Tang Annals not consulted directly.

audits.claim: Chuba (dress): Smithsonian describes a right-side fastening; several material constructions; and 'thousands of years' continuity language that does not prove an unchanged ancient garment.
audits.source_locator: page body, paragraphs 1-2; Catalog No. CFV11277; Research: Khamo Kyi; Editing: Jackson Harvey; (c) 2019 Smithsonian Institution
audits.source_excerpt: Tibetan robes are distinct with their wide fronts and wide waists, which are buttoned on the right side.
audits.basis: Page lists five chuba forms (woolen with inner sheep fur, pulu, lambskin, sheepskin, light robes) and states 'Tibetans have been making and wearing robes for thousands of years' - the entry quotes and correctly qualifies that continuity language. Couples dress with terminology and materials.
audits.access_limit: Curated educational description page for a video; the video itself was not watched; the page does not document regional or status rules.

audits.claim: The title Dalai Lama was bestowed on the Third in the line; earlier numbering must not imply predecessors used the title in their lifetimes.
audits.source_excerpt: The third in the line, Sonam Gyatso, was given the title of the Dalai Lama.
audits.basis: Names/institution/era coupling: the same paragraph assigns the recognition system's start to Gedun Gyatso in the fifteenth century, with numbering retrospective; the entry's phrasing matches.
audits.access_limit: Institutional self-account; partisan in recognition disputes, as the entry already qualifies.

audits.claim: Era table: Central Tibetan Ganden Phodrang rule, 1642-1959 on the plateau.
audits.source_excerpt: The Fifth Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, established the Gaden Phodrang Government in 1642
audits.basis: 1642 start confirmed (source spells 'Gaden Phodrang'). The statement instead counts '369 years since 1642' to 2011, an institutional leadership claim spanning exile; the entry's plateau scoping avoids that extension, and the 1959 endpoint is standard historiography not asserted by this source - not re-verified here.
audits.access_limit: Institutional self-account; the 1959 plateau endpoint has no retrieved primary support in this recheck.

audits.claim: The Golden Urn belongs to late-eighteenth-century Qing intervention, not the institution's medieval beginning.
audits.source_excerpt: This proposal included the suggestion of picking lots from a Golden Urn to decide on the recognition of the reincarnations of the Dalai Lamas, Panchen Lamas and Hutuktus
audits.basis: Preceded by 'During the conflict between Tibet and the Gurkhas (1791-93) ... afterwards Manchu officials made a 29-point proposal': supports the entry's late-eighteenth-century dating; era/institution coupling.
audits.access_limit: Institutional account of a Qing intervention; no Qing archival source retrieved.

audits.claim: Exact use of the Golden Urn in individual successions remains (to-verify) against case evidence and Oidtmann (2018), not only the 2011 institutional statement.
audits.source_excerpt: The Golden Urn system was actually used only in the cases of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dalai Lamas.
audits.basis: The statement gives an emic account of specific succession use (it adds that the Twelfth had already been recognized before the procedure, leaving effectively one Dalai Lama recognized by the method), but the entry's open question is directed at case evidence and Oidtmann (2018); that archival cross-check was not performed in this recheck.
audits.access_limit: Partisan institutional source; no neutral case-evidence source retrieved; Oidtmann (2018) full text not retrieved.

audits.claim: g.yung drung: endurance/eternity vocabulary in early royal contexts; also names the swastika sign; varied Buddhist translation uses; later central to Yungdrung Bon.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/tibet.md:64 and 93 (section 3 table row; section 5 semantic-history bullet)
audits.source_excerpt: Eternity seems to be the general meaning of yungdrung in the early religion. In addition, the word was associated with the ancient Indo-European swastika design, which in Tibet was the graphic symbol of the eternal.
audits.basis: Language/myth/era coupling: the post also records varied Buddhist uses (to translate nirvana, samyak, and sanatana), later standardization, and that 'From the 11th century it became a central concept of the later Bon tradition' - Yungdrung Bon. Matches both entry rows.
audits.access_limit: Specialist research blog post by Sam van Schaik citing Dunhuang manuscripts (e.g. IOL Tib J 339); manuscripts not independently inspected.

audits.claim: Prayer-wheel rows: one turn equals recitation of the enclosed repetitions; microfilm as well as manuscripts; Nagarjuna-Padmasambhava lineage narrative; donor motivated by fishing wealth; water/wind/heat-driven forms; healing claims present but excluded from use.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved_full_text (edited transcript, teaching at Land of Medicine Buddha, June 1994)
audits.source_excerpt: Turning a prayer wheel containing 100 million om mani padme hum mantras accumulates the same merit as having recited 100 million om mani padme hums.
audits.basis: Transcript also: 'it also contains many mantras on microfilm'; 'Nagarjuna gave the practice to Lion-face Dakini, who gave it to Padmasambhava'; the fishing-family donor; 'There are earth, water, fire and wind prayer wheels'; and an AIDS/cancer healing passage - the entry uses it as emic testimony, not efficacy. Specific origin date of the first physical wheel: not addressed, so the entry's (to-verify) marker correctly remains.
audits.access_limit: Practitioner testimony; edited transcript by the Lama Yeshe Wisdom Archive; supernatural claims not independently verifiable and not treated as such.

audits.claim: Values can reverse: Yongdan (2018) documents otter fur's prestige and the changed consumption associated with the Dalai Lama's 2006 criticism.

audits.source_excerpt: Before 2006, otter pelts, the skins of carnivorous mammals from the Lutrinae family, were considered to be among the most precious and sought-after commodities in Tibet
audits.basis: Abstract continues that after the Dalai Lama criticised wild animal fur use in 2006, 'most Tibetans not only stopped wearing otter fur', some burning pelts; matches the entry's dated reversal. Era/value-dress coupling.
audits.access_limit: Abstract only; full article paywalled (Brill access options/institutional login); page numbers 177-198 not inspected.
